tier_reason: The README Benchmarks section compares enchantum with magic_enum (plus simple_enum and conjure_enum) on compile time, object size and executable size, and every number in claimed_speedup matches the tables; the generator benchmarks/gen.py is public and its four test cases match the README parameters. Compilers (GCC 14.2.0, Clang 20.1.2, MSVC 19.44) and -O3 / /Ox are stated, but no CPU model, no command lines and no competitor library versions, and the runs are first-party, so it stays C.

corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark; CPU model, exact command lines and the versions of magic_enum, simple_enum and conjure_enum are not stated, so it falls short of tier A, although the generator (benchmarks/gen.py) is public and its four test cases (Small 200 enums x 16 members, range -128..128; Big 32 x 200, -256..256; Large Range 200 x 16, -1024..1024; Ideal Range 100 x 50, 0..50) match the README table. The bold headline numbers are with the out-of-bounds check disabled (ENCHANTUM_CHECK_OUT_OF_BOUNDS_BY=0), which gen.py does not set, so they need an extra define; the parenthesised values are the default setting (2) and are about 1.2x to 2.1x slower on GCC (MSVC Small 37.4 vs 15.8 s, MSVC Ideal Range 16 vs 5.8 s), so the default-configuration win over magic_enum is smaller (GCC Small 5.7x rather than 7.8x; MSVC Ideal Range 16 vs 17.9 s, near parity). simple_enum is faster on the Ideal Range case on all three compilers (GCC 2.7 vs 3 s, Clang 2.3 vs 2.9 s, MSVC 4.7 vs 5.8 s); the author notes simple_enum was given first/last members spanning the whole reflection range, which the README itself calls a misuse of that library. magic_enum is given the same ranges as enchantum (up to -1024..1024, where it timed out after 20 minutes), far above its default -128..127; the Ideal Range case (0..50), where magic_enum is only 2.7x slower with the check disabled, is the least range-inflated comparison. Each generated file calls to_string once per enum through a volatile; there is no runtime lookup benchmark and no comparison with a hand-written switch or string_view table. Object and executable sizes were measured on Clang only. The README links a post by Vittorio Romeo (a friend of the author) on the compile-time cost of enum-to-string with C++26 reflection versus older methods via reddit; reddit and the aggregator copy (feedbagel.com) were blocked here, so it was not read and no independent reproduction was found.

notes: Numbers verified against the README tables; gen.py read and consistent with the test-case table. Metadata confirmed on github.com: MIT, 162 stars, 15 forks, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-09-16 ('Add nlohmann header'), active. Shortcomings for the orchestrator: CPU and library versions unstated; headline numbers use a non-default out-of-bounds setting that gen.py does not apply; simple_enum beats it on the Ideal Range case; magic_enum compared at ranges far above its default; compile-time only, no runtime numbers.

tier_reason: doc/callback-benchmark.md compares cpgf GCallback/GCallbackList with libsigc++ 2.2.8 and Boost.Signals2 1.46.0, and every number in claimed_speedup matches its table; the harness is public (test/benchmark/callback/benchmarkcallback.cpp plus benchmarkcallback.h), and compilers (VC 9 -O2 with _SECURE_SCL=0, MinGW GCC 4.5.2 -O3) and CPU (Pentium Dual E2180 2 GHz) are stated, which meets A.

corrections.caveats: The numbers date from about 2011 (Pentium Dual E2180, Windows XP SP2, VC 9, MinGW GCC 4.5.2, Boost 1.46.0, libsigc++ 2.2.8) and the page itself says newer hardware will produce quite different results; newer Boost.Signals2 and libsigc++ releases were not measured. The harness runs one generation (Iterates_Generations = 1), timed with clock() at millisecond resolution, so each cell is a single run with no repeat or variance. In the single-slot rows the Boost column invokes a boost::signals2::slot object directly (slot::operator() locks tracked objects on every call), not a signal; only the signal rows use the default mutex-protected boost::signals2::signal. Single-slot cpgf calls are at parity with libsigc++ and sometimes slightly slower (VC 9: inline 781 vs 766 ms, virtual 719 vs 672 ms, functor 468 vs 438 ms; GCC: 1047 vs 1000 ms inline) and 10 to 22 times slower than an inlinable native call (46-47 ms); the clear wins are against Boost.Signals2 and in signal emission with few slots (5 slots 641 vs 2734 ms libsigc++), shrinking to 1.17x against libsigc++ at 50 slots. The page says FastDelegate code from CodeProject was 'one time faster' (about twice as fast) than cpgf callback and libsigc++ slots but left it out of the table; the harness also needs FastDelegate.h and delegate.hpp unless NO_FD and NO_SR are defined, and it includes the header under a cpgf/testcase/benchmark/ path while the repo keeps it next to the .cpp, with no build script for the benchmark. No comparison against std::function or a modern signal library. The project is discontinued: its README says it is not continued and points callback users to the author's eventpp (already listed as eventpp::SpinLock) and reflection users to metapp. The benchmark covers only the callback component, not the reflection, serialization or script-binding parts. Filed under smart-pointers-and-refcount, where the catalogue files signal and delegate libraries (same placement as larspensjo/simplesignal and bdiamand/delegate). The harness source was read but not built or rerun.

notes: Every claimed number re-derived from the page table (for example 8797/641 = 13.7x and 2734/641 = 4.3x). Metadata confirmed on github.com: Apache-2.0, 221 stars, 61 forks, not archived or a fork, last commit 2022-05-22, abandoned (README says the project is not continued). Not a duplicate of eventpp, which is a separate successor project. Shortcomings: 2011-era toolchain and library versions, single clock() run per cell, parity or slight losses against libsigc++ on single-slot calls, Boost single-slot rows time a signals2::slot rather than a signal.
